When a film is remade for a foreign market, translators must decide how much of the original's cultural texture to preserve. Keep every local reference intact, and the new audience may feel excluded by jokes and allusions it cannot parse. Strip them all away, and the story loses the specificity that made it feel true in the first place. The most successful adaptations tend to occupy a middle ground, replacing references that would baffle viewers while retaining enough of the source's flavour to keep it recognisably itself. Localisation, in this view, is less a technical act of substitution than an editorial judgment about which meanings can travel and which must be rebuilt.

Film festivals present themselves as showcases for bold, uncommercial work, yet the economics tell a subtler story. A prize at a major festival can turn an unknown title into a distributor's target overnight, and the buzz of a premiere is a marketing asset that money alone cannot buy. Filmmakers, in turn, tailor their work and their timing to the festival calendar, chasing the validation that unlocks funding for the next project. Far from standing apart from the market, the festival has become one of its most efficient engines.

**Which option best summarises the paragraph?**

Recommendation algorithms promise to free listeners from the tyranny of the mainstream, surfacing obscure artists a radio station would never play. In practice the effect is often the reverse. Because the systems learn from what most people already enjoy, they tend to funnel millions of users toward the same safe, familiar tracks. The obscure song still exists in the catalogue, but the machinery is built to bury it. What looks like infinite choice can quietly narrow into a single well-worn groove.

**Which option best summarises the paragraph?**

The idea of the lone author has always been something of a convenient fiction, but franchise cinema has made its emptiness impossible to ignore. A modern blockbuster is assembled by hundreds of hands, its script revised by committee, its images finished by studios on three continents, its shape set as much by a release schedule as by any vision. To ask who its author is may simply be the wrong question. The more honest one is whether authorship, as we have understood it, describes anything real about how such films come to exist.
